name: Insulin and Beta Cell Replacement
blurb: Once-weekly insulin, new formulations and replacing insulin producing cells.
title: Insulin and Beta Cell Replacement
answer: Insulin is changing in two directions. Once-weekly basal insulins, insulin icodec (Awiqli) and insulin efsitora alfa (Onswik), were approved in the United States in 2026 for type 2 diabetes, cutting basal injections from seven a week to one. Further out, stem cell derived islets aim to replace the beta cells that make insulin.

sections.body: Weekly insulin may suit people who struggle with daily injections; ask your doctor whether switching makes sense for you.
sections.heading: What it means for patients

siblings.name: Kidney Protection and Diabetic Kidney Disease

explainer:
Basal insulin provides a steady background level of insulin through the day and night. Weekly insulins bind to proteins in the blood and release slowly, so one injection covers seven days. Trials showed glucose control similar to daily basal insulin; doses are adjusted weekly, and how to handle missed doses and hypoglycemia differs from daily insulin.

Beta cell replacement aims higher. Islet transplants from donors can restore insulin production but are scarce and need lifelong immunosuppressive drugs. Stem cell derived islets can be made in large numbers; early trials show they can restore insulin production, and research is working on encapsulation devices and gene edited cells that could avoid immunosuppression.

developments.text: The FDA approved Onswik (insulin efsitora alfa), the second once-weekly insulin for type 2 diabetes, following Awiqli (insulin icodec).
In an early trial of zimislecel, stem cell derived fully differentiated islets, 10 of 12 participants with type 1 diabetes were insulin independent at one year.
